extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; school authorities/printers/oculists, volcanologists, and oceanographers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical standards for designing and selecting school-books and classroom environments to preserve pupils' eyesight (typography, spacing, line length, lighting, furniture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of volcanic bombs (contents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their contents may be divided into two classes: 1. Scoriaceous vesicular lava, identical in composition with the external shell. 2. Miscellaneous, such as altered masses of lapilli, loose blocks of foreign materials caught up in the current of lava.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these classes to identify and interpret spherical lava fragments ('volcanic bombs') found around volcanoes; consider nucleus and concretionary processes in origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility of airborne cooling origin for volcanic bombs
rubrics_metrics.description: The common idea that volcanic bombs are formed by masses ejected to great heights and cooling as they whirl through the atmosphere seems improbable, because on falling they would inevitably smash into a thousand fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor a concretionary origin (solidification around a cool nucleus with surface crusting) unless evidence strongly supports survival of fragments through aerial travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of inner vs outer cone slope
rubrics_metrics.description: The inner (chimney) side often retains a greater slope than the outer because fusion/cementing of fragments by intense heat and presence of lava solders masses together; when the internal fluid column disappears, a lining forms by semifusion of superficial components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slope differences and signs of semifusion/cementing to infer internal thermal history and stability of cone walls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical chimney (vent) geometry of cones
rubrics_metrics.description: Many craters show a cavity whose sides descend for a certain distance at a moderate angle (roughly 45°), then suddenly increase to nearly a perpendicular, producing a basin-like cavity with the volcanic vent at its center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this funnel/basin geometry as common in cones built largely of ejecta and lapilli; useful when predicting where new cones may build within the basin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentric repetition of cones and craters
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials ejected by a comparatively quiescent volcano tend to build up a fresh cone occupying the basin; concentric arrangements of cones and craters may be repeated many times (e.g., Somma/Vesuvius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mapping volcano morphology, look for concentric nested cones indicating multiple eruptive episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of vent migration (eccentric venting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vent position may shift and become eccentric, producing overlapping of the newer cone upon the older; lava-stream abundance may be greater on the side nearest the active bocca.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret asymmetric lava distribution and overlapping cones as evidence of vent migration; use to reconstruct eruptive history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of vapor in maintaining a vent
rubrics_metrics.description: Vapor is the real agent in keeping a vent clear: vast bubbles rise through viscous mass, bursting at the surface, keeping up the temperature of the lava-column and preventing permanent stagnation; vapor is often seen as white clouds carried by wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observations of vapor behavior to assess ongoing vent activity and likelihood of continued lava ascent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation and morphology of fumaroles
rubrics_metrics.description: Fumaroles result from vapor and lava acting together; they vary from spire-like to miter-like (when escaping along a fissure); size varies from 12 inches to 30 feet and upward; built layer by layer by spasmodic puffs forcing small quantities of lava to the aperture which rapidly cools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify fumarole types and their layered, imbricated exterior as indicators of formation mechanism; measure bore and wall smoothness when extinct to assess past vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria distinguishing upheaval vs ejecta cone-formation theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Upheavalists: earth-crust surrounding vent bodily lifted into a dome/bubble, subjacent rock would have a quaquaversal or periclinal dip away on all sides from the chimney. Opponents: entire bulk of mountain attributed to ejecta; basement beds show dips produced by pressure and excavation tending to make them dip toward the vent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed bedding dips (away from vent vs toward vent), presence/absence of large ejecta deposits, and other field facts to adjudicate between the two models; recognize that some cones may show mixed evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapidity of cone formation (field example standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volcanic cones can be raised very rapidly—example: Monte Nuovo (456 feet) raised in about four days (Sept. 30, 1538), produced largely by fragmentary ejecta with no stream of lava.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to extremely rapid cone formation in field interpretations when supported by historical or stratigraphic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of myopia relevant to schools
rubrics_metrics.description: All protracted looking at close objects may contribute; active causes include badly-constructed school-benches, imperfect lighting, too much reading, bad writing, and bad type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing school environments for eye-health risk, examine furniture ergonomics, lighting, reading load, handwriting practices, and the typography used in texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement standard for visible letter size (use of 'n')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not judge type by printer's 'em'; instead measure the visible letter (use the letter 'n' as the regular, symmetrical standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the visible 'n' measurement when specifying or inspecting type sizes for legibility and eye health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum recommended letter height for school-books
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters which are less than a millimetre and a half in height will finally prove injurious to the eye; many school-books use nonpareil (1 mm) which is too small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject school-texts with letter heights under 1.5 mm; prefer those using 2 mm letters or larger when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority recommendation on acceptable type sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers should throw out every school-book in which the letters are less than a millimetre and a half high, and should give the preference to establishments which do not use letters of less than two millimetres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: School authorities should inspect and preferentially procure textbooks meeting the ≥2 mm letter-height standard; absolute minimum 1.5 mm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlinear spacing (leading) for ease of reading
rubrics_metrics.description: A book is well-leaded when the interlinear space, measured by the shorter letters, amounts to three millimetres; the narrowest interval permitted should be two and a half millimetres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify around 3 mm interline space as ideal for school texts; never allow less than 2.5 mm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stroke (stroke-width) thickness minimum
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters having a stroke of less than one fourth of a millimetre in thickness should not be admitted into school-books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify minimum stroke thickness ≈0.25 mm to ensure clear letter-form rendition and retinal imprinting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between letters (kerning/letter-spacing) for legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ample space should be allowed between letters; Laboulaye recommended that every two letters should be separated by a clear space at least as broad as the distance between the two strokes of the 'n'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use generous inter-letter spacing—roughly at least the width between strokes of an 'n'—to reduce crowding and visual confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line length recommendation for school-books
rubrics_metrics.description: The most suitable length of lines for school-books appears to be about ninety millimetres, or three and a half inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design schoolbook pages with shorter line lengths (~90 mm) to reduce eye excursions and reading fatigue, especially for near-sighted readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print contrast and paper quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Legibility is improved by contrast; the darker the print and the clearer the paper, the easier the reading. When lines are close together or the matter printed 'solid', the eyes become tired sooner because contrast is lessened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify high contrast printing on clear paper and avoid tightly-set ('solid') type; favor darker ink and cleaner paper surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic form considerations (Roman vs German letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Javal observed Roman rectangular letters liable to be reduced in apparent size and have corners seem rounded by irradiation from white paper, recommending thickening cross-strokes at ends; many physicians think German letters more tiresome, but large/thick print and far-apart lines mitigate this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using Roman type, consider slight thickening of cross-strokes; ensure any script (Roman or German) used in schoolbooks is sufficiently large, thick, and well-led to avoid additional eye strain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting standard for schoolrooms
rubrics_metrics.description: At least thirty square inches of window-space should be provided for each square foot of floor-space; more light is better, and care must be taken that pupils are not exposed to glare while others sit in obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design or retrofit classrooms to maximize even natural lighting (aim ~30 in² window per ft² floor area) and avoid extreme contrast/glare for some pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of classroom lighting (avoid glare/obscurity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many schoolrooms pupils nearest the windows may sit in a glare while those farthest away cannot study for the obscurity; there can never be too much light in a schoolroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange seating, windows, and artificial lighting to provide even illumination across the room; minimize glare and ensure distant benches have adequate light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ergonomics: school-benches and furniture construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Badly-constructed school-benches are among the active causes that tend to produce myopy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect and improve bench and desk design to promote proper posture and viewing distance; include ergonomic standards in school procurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical policy for school authorities inspecting textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers should go through every school-book with a millimetre-rule and throw out all in which the letters are less than a millimetre and a half high, and should give preference to those using letters of not less than two millimetres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a millimetre-rule inspection protocol for textbook approval and procurement focused on letter height and spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lead-line technique for shallow depth soundings
rubrics_metrics.description: For ordinary purposes in depths of not more than twelve or fifteen fathoms, the ordinary hand lead-line (20–25 fathoms long) is effective and correct; accurate soundings to 30–40 fathoms obtained by reducing vessel speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply traditional lead-line methods for shallow coastal sounding, using reduced ship speed for greater accuracy when depth allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep-sea sounding methods and instrumentation adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: In ocean-water (depths of 2–3,000 fathoms) the vessel must be kept stationary and heavier weights used; Americans used fine twine and heavy weight (sacrificed) to obviate rope overweight; iron wire introduced ~1850 to mitigate line weight problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very deep soundings adopt heavier shots, consider sacrificial fine twine or iron wire to avoid cumulative rope weight errors, and maintain station during soundings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using rate-of-line-out observation to detect bottom
rubrics_metrics.description: Observing the rate at which successive equal lengths of line pass out has been found useful where ordinary observation/feeling does not suffice to indicate when the shot has reached bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor payout speed changes as an additional sign of bottom contact, especially in very deep soundings where feel is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design criteria for bottom-sampling apparatus (sample size and retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Burke's apparatus used a cannon-ball and rod with disengaging hooks to bring up mud in quill tubes; Hydra had butterfly valves and captured bottom-water but brought small samples; Bailey used a larger tube to bring more considerable samples—chief objection to earlier machines was smallness of samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sampling gear that secures sufficiently large and intact bottom samples (larger tube diameters, reliable closing valves) over devices that capture only minute quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-lake sounding apparatus design (tube+sinker approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's apparatus: straight brass tube ~1 inch diameter with a shoulder; cylindrical lead sinker slips over tube; lower portion unscrews to squeeze out mud; tubes bury readily in soft mud and bring up considerable samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small-lake work use narrow-diameter tubular corers with removable lower segments and weighted shoulders to obtain cohesive mud samples without complex release mechanisms.
